text: Hello, my name is Thorsten Dieckoh, and I'm excited to be here to talk to you about
the data transcription from insect specimen labels and the
itemization of those data into Darwin Core fields using machine learning.
Currently, at the Smithsonian National Museum of Natural History, we are digitizing
part of our insect collection, and we're focusing on pollinators.
We have about 2.4 million pollinating insects in our collection that are
preserved or mounted on pins, and we have funding in hand
to digitize about 360,000 of the specimens.
We're focusing on bees, beetles, butterflies, and flies,
and we will digitize all specimens and all species in selected
genera to accomplish this goal. We will
share all data or are already currently sharing those
data in the public domain, both the images and the data, of course.
This project started in June of 2025.
We are using a pinned insect digitization conveyor developed
by Pictory, and we have a setup in our museum where we have three
operators feeding the machine, which allows us to digitize up to
1,500 specimens per day.
You have heard a talk earlier in the week by Jessica Bird about this conveyor
project and some of the digital workflows that we have developed.
I have also given a talk about this bigger project at the Spinach meetings
two weeks ago in Cape Town, and at my last slide of this presentation, I have a
link to that presentation slides as well, if you wanted to learn more about this
project in general.
To make sure we're all on the same page, I just wanted to briefly introduce what a
pinned insect actually is. We see here on the top a
specimen that is photographed with its label attached to
the pin, and then the label laid out on the side.
And on the bottom, those images actually are
photos that are coming off the conveyor and are delivered to us by Pictory,
which is a lateral view of the insect, a dorsal view, and then a frontal view.
And on the right-hand side, the lower right-hand side, you can see the labels, how
they are photographed for this particular specimen, and how they are delivered to
us from Pictory.
The current project uses a human transcription, and
we
have been working with an external vendor called Alembo.
This human transcription was the choice of method at the time,
but Jessica and I decided we would also like to explore a little
bit more machine learning and new technologies to get the data off the
labels. So, for example, in the human transcription, there is no interpretation
of the data.
And that means, for example, an abbreviation of CA, which stands for California,
the state of California here in the United States, it would be transcribed as
CA but not interpreted to mean California.
And on the bottom left, you can see a screenshot of our
transcription QC tool called Osprey.
On the left-hand side is a photo of the two
labels associated with a particular specimen, and on the right-hand side, the text
that is fielded into Darwin Core fields.
So Jessica and I started a collaboration with colleagues
from the University of Maryland, both in computer science and entomology.
And this project of extracting data from
digitized labels was an undergraduate capstone project in the fall of
2025. And our goal was to actually not just work on the
extraction of the letters of the words from labels, but go beyond and actually
itemize these into Darwin Core fields.
The digitization projects across the museum, both previously or now with the
conveyor, obviously
generate many photos of labels. And on the left-hand side, the top left, you can
see an example of our boutique photography when we, as researchers, take
photographs of specimens for our own uses,
and that's how they often laid out.
We have a policy in our museum in entomology that whenever a
specimen from our collection is photographed, the labels also have to be
photographed. And on the right-hand side, you can see an example of
photos of labels that are coming off the conveyor that I mentioned before.
Recently, there have been a few publications that focus on
exactly the same idea of extracting the data using
machine learning.
But the two citations that I have on the bottom of my screen, they
are not going beyond that, the text extraction, and putting it into a long
string and not itemizing those data into Darwin Core fields.
So this is one of the goals that we had in our project.
Our tool that we call LaBeLLum has three main steps, and I want to walk you
through for the next few slides about these steps, what actually happens behind the
scenes. So the first step is the label extraction, and you can see on the left-hand
side two sets of labels photographed from two different specimens with three and
six labels attached to them
respectively.
We're using a computer vision model called YOLO to actually extract now
the
individual labels from the
entire photo. And our initial accuracy was about 95% of
that extraction.
So that's very high, and it works very well.
On the right-hand side, the next step is the text transcription, now taking the
letters and the words off those individualized labels and putting them
into a field, meaning that all the
letters and words are
itemized per label. And you can see on the right-hand side
a photo of four labels, and then below you see in
columns the different fields that have the text that is actually
100% matched to what is shown in the label.
We're using a lightweight Gemini model and the
Gemma 312B
machine learning tool behind it.
Our initial accuracy was about 82%, so there's certainly room for
improvement of that step as well.
The next step is now what we call the bucket extraction, and this is
to now get the data, the
words that are taken off the labels into structured Darwin Core
fields. And here we use, again, the Gemini model provided by
Google, and we have a set of Darwin Core fields that
we think are important for the labels in our
entomology collection to do the basic capturing of the
information. And you can here see the same example of the photo of the
labels on the left, and then on the right-hand side, the now Darwin Core
fielding of those
words and letters
into the right categories. And there's only one arrow that is shown here in that

The prompts that we are using
are shown here in some overview. We obviously give context to the whole
project. We use controlled vocabularies for the country names,
and we use Darwin Core field definitions to tell the
model what information is behind these different
Darwin Core fields. And then at the bottom, an example of just the output
format that we request
to give us from the model.

of our tool so far was to compare
100 label images versus the 100 records that actually make

in the labels. However, obviously on the labels, there's no information about

high accuracy of 99% and 98%. So there's no problem
at this particular point.

two analyses
refer to the genus and the specific epithet that is
found on those labels. And you can see here we have two issues of
28% of
the two are not getting the correct information.

and on the right that there is actually no species and genus

higher because it would be 62 plus 28% or 65 plus
28% of accuracy of

correctly
taken into account and transcribed.
We have two examples here. So on the right-hand side, we have an issue of
35%, there's no text extracted, and here's an example of one of those

6%, we have an error in which the number seven, which is right here,

time. So here there's obviously space for improvement, and we have
to find ways how to improve the unique identifier, which is obviously very

data to have the correct number associated with the data.
So in summary, we need to improve some of our
prompting for the Darwin Core fields and work on some other refinements, and we are
doing that right now. We hope to develop Labellum as
a self-contained tool to run on a laptop and a desktop computer.
And we plan to publish our results and then share with the naturalistic
collection community so other museums, other collections can utilize our
tool for exactly the thousands of
digitized labels being transcribed with the use of Labellum and then
come up with Darwin Core compliant data for import into the database or for
